stem: A technician plans to 'delete the files and quick-format' hard drives that held confidential data before sending them offsite. Why is this approach inadequate?

options.text: Deletion and quick-format leave data recoverable due to data remanence
options.rationale: Standard deletion and quick-format only remove pointers/file tables; the underlying data remains and can be recovered, which is the data remanence problem.

options.text: Quick-format encrypts the data too strongly to read
options.rationale: Quick-format does not encrypt anything; it merely clears the file allocation structures, leaving data intact.

options.text: The drives will be physically destroyed by formatting
options.rationale: Formatting does not physically destroy media or its data content.

options.text: It removes the data but takes too long
options.rationale: The issue is not time; it is that the data is not actually removed and remains recoverable.

stem: A batch of solid-state drives (SSDs) that held sensitive data must be sanitized before disposal. Which method is BEST suited to SSDs?

options.text: Cryptographic erase or physical destruction
options.rationale: SSDs are not reliably sanitized by degaussing or simple overwrite due to wear-leveling; crypto-erase (destroying keys) or destruction is appropriate.

options.text: Degaussing with a magnetic field
options.rationale: Degaussing works on magnetic media but is ineffective on flash-based SSDs, which store data electronically.

options.text: A single quick-format
options.rationale: Quick-format leaves data recoverable and does not address SSD remanence.

options.text: Deleting the partition table
options.rationale: Removing the partition table does not erase the underlying flash cells; data remains recoverable.

stem: Magnetic drives holding confidential data are being returned to an external leasing vendor. Which sanitization level is the MOST appropriate minimum?

options.text: Purging (e.g., degaussing) because the media is leaving the organization
options.rationale: When media is released outside organizational control, purging that resists laboratory recovery is the minimum appropriate level.

options.text: Clearing by a single overwrite is sufficient
options.rationale: Clearing blocks standard recovery but is generally reserved for media that stays inside the organization, not media released externally.

options.text: A quick-format only
options.rationale: Quick-format does not remove data and is far below the required level for external release.

options.text: No sanitization, since the vendor is trusted
options.rationale: Trust in a vendor does not justify releasing recoverable confidential data; sanitization is still required.

stem: For media that held the organization's most highly classified data and will never be reused, which sanitization approach provides the highest assurance?

options.text: Physical destruction (shredding, incineration, or pulverizing)
options.rationale: Destroying the media provides the highest assurance that data cannot be recovered, appropriate for the most sensitive, non-reusable media.

options.text: A single-pass overwrite
options.rationale: A single overwrite (clearing) is a lower assurance level than destruction and inappropriate for the highest classification.

options.text: Moving the files to the recycle bin
options.rationale: The recycle bin does not remove data at all and offers no assurance.

options.text: Renaming the files to hide them
options.rationale: Renaming does nothing to remove or protect the underlying data.

stem: An organization wants to ensure every storage device is properly sanitized before disposal, but devices sometimes go missing. What must be in place FIRST to make this reliable?

options.text: An accurate asset inventory tracking every device through its lifecycle
options.rationale: Without knowing what media exists and where it is, the organization cannot guarantee each device is accounted for and sanitized.

options.text: A faster shredder
options.rationale: A faster shredder does not help if devices are unaccounted for and never reach the shredder.

options.text: More cloud storage
options.rationale: Adding cloud storage does not solve tracking of physical media disposal.

options.text: A stronger firewall
options.rationale: A firewall protects network traffic, not the tracking and disposal of physical media.

stem: A company moves data to an IaaS cloud provider and assumes the provider now handles all security. Under the shared responsibility model, which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: The customer remains responsible for its data, access control, and configuration
options.rationale: Under shared responsibility, the provider secures the underlying infrastructure while the customer retains responsibility for data, access, and configuration.

options.text: The provider assumes full responsibility for the customer's data protection
options.rationale: This is the trap; the provider secures infrastructure but does not take over the customer's data and configuration duties.

options.text: Security responsibilities disappear once data is in the cloud
options.rationale: Responsibilities are shared, not eliminated; the customer still owns significant obligations.

options.text: The customer is only responsible for physical data center security
options.rationale: Physical data center security is the provider's responsibility; the customer handles data, access, and configuration.

stem: Degaussing is an effective sanitization method for which type of media?

options.text: Magnetic media such as hard disk drives and tapes
options.rationale: Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field to erase magnetic media; it is effective on magnetic disks and tapes.

options.text: Solid-state drives (SSDs)
options.rationale: SSDs store data in flash cells electronically, so magnetic degaussing does not erase them.

options.text: Optical media such as DVDs
options.rationale: Optical discs are not magnetic; degaussing has no effect and destruction is used instead.

options.text: Paper documents
options.rationale: Paper is not magnetic media; shredding, not degaussing, is used for paper.

stem: Employees are installing unapproved 'shadow' software on company systems, creating licensing and security risks. Which resource-protection practice BEST addresses this?

options.text: Maintaining a software asset inventory and controlling/allowlisting approved software
options.rationale: Tracking installed software and restricting installation to approved applications curbs shadow IT and its licensing and security risks.

options.text: Encrypting all hard drives
options.rationale: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest but does not detect or prevent unauthorized software installation.

options.text: Adding more RAM to workstations
options.rationale: Hardware capacity is unrelated to controlling unapproved software.

options.text: Lengthening password expiration intervals
options.rationale: Password policy changes do not address shadow software installation.

stem: Which practice BEST supports proper handling of removable media containing sensitive data?

options.text: Labeling media by classification and controlling its storage and transport
options.rationale: Marking media by sensitivity and controlling how it is stored and moved ensures it is handled per its classification.

options.text: Leaving media unlabeled to avoid drawing attention
options.rationale: Unlabeled media leads to mishandling because handlers cannot know its sensitivity.

options.text: Storing sensitive media in unlocked common areas
options.rationale: Uncontrolled storage exposes sensitive media to theft or loss.

options.text: Allowing anyone to transport media without tracking
options.rationale: Untracked transport breaks accountability and risks loss of sensitive media.

stem: What PRIMARILY determines how strictly a given asset or piece of media should be protected and sanitized?

options.text: The classification/sensitivity of the data it holds
options.rationale: Protection and sanitization requirements scale with data sensitivity; classification drives the appropriate handling and disposal method.

options.text: The physical color of the device
options.rationale: The device's color has no bearing on protection requirements.

options.text: The brand of the manufacturer
options.rationale: Manufacturer branding does not determine required protection levels.

options.text: The age of the employee assigned to it
options.rationale: Employee age is irrelevant to how an asset must be protected.

stem: What is data remanence?

options.text: Residual data that remains on media after ordinary deletion or formatting
options.rationale: Data remanence is leftover recoverable data that persists unless proper sanitization is applied.

options.text: Data that has been fully and irreversibly destroyed
options.rationale: Remanence is the opposite — data that survives and can be recovered, not data that is destroyed.

options.text: The maximum amount of data a drive can hold
options.rationale: That describes storage capacity, not remanence.

options.text: Encrypted data that cannot be decrypted
options.rationale: Remanence concerns recoverable residual data, not undecryptable ciphertext.

stem: A fleet of self-encrypting drives must be quickly sanitized so the data becomes unrecoverable. Which method BEST accomplishes this efficiently?

options.text: Cryptographic erase — destroy the encryption keys so the ciphertext is unrecoverable
options.rationale: Destroying the keys on a self-encrypting drive renders all stored ciphertext unrecoverable quickly, a recognized purge method.

options.text: Overwriting the entire drive several times manually
options.rationale: Multi-pass overwrite is slower and, on SSDs, may miss wear-leveled cells; crypto-erase is the efficient, appropriate method here.

options.text: Degaussing the drives
options.rationale: Degaussing does not work on the flash storage of self-encrypting SSDs.

options.text: Deleting the encryption software
options.rationale: Removing software does not destroy the keys or the recoverable data; the ciphertext and keys may remain.

stem: A hard drive will be reassigned to another employee within the same secure department. Which sanitization level is generally the BEST fit?

options.text: Clearing (overwriting) is acceptable because the media stays within the organization
options.rationale: Clearing blocks standard recovery and is appropriate when media remains under organizational control and is reused internally.

options.text: Physical destruction of the drive
options.rationale: Destroying a reusable drive intended for internal reassignment is unnecessary and wasteful when clearing suffices.

options.text: No sanitization at all
options.rationale: Even internal reassignment requires sanitization so the new user cannot access the prior user's data.

options.text: Only renaming the previous user's folders
options.rationale: Renaming does not remove the data and leaves it accessible to the next user.

stem: Why is an accurate hardware and software asset inventory considered a PRIMARY foundation of resource protection?

options.text: Because you cannot protect, patch, or securely dispose of assets you do not know you have
options.rationale: An inventory is prerequisite knowledge; unknown assets cannot be protected, patched, classified, or sanitized.

options.text: Because inventories automatically encrypt all data
options.rationale: An inventory records assets; it does not perform encryption.

options.text: Because an inventory removes the need for access controls
options.rationale: Inventories complement, not replace, access controls.

options.text: Because inventories guarantee no asset will ever fail
options.rationale: Inventories track assets; they do not prevent hardware failure.

stem: Which method is LEAST effective for sanitizing a solid-state drive that held sensitive data?

options.text: Degaussing the drive
options.rationale: Degaussing relies on magnetism and has no effect on flash-based SSDs, making it the least effective method listed for an SSD.

options.text: Cryptographic erase of the drive's keys
options.rationale: Crypto-erase is an effective, recognized method for SSDs, so it is not the least effective.

options.text: Physical destruction of the drive
options.rationale: Destruction is highly effective for SSDs, providing the highest assurance.

options.text: Vendor-supported secure erase command
options.rationale: A proper secure-erase built for the SSD is effective, unlike degaussing.

stem: In an IaaS deployment, which responsibility clearly remains with the customer rather than the cloud provider?

options.text: Configuring access controls and protecting the customer's own data
options.rationale: Under the shared responsibility model, customers retain responsibility for their data, identity/access configuration, and application settings.

options.text: Physical security of the data center facility
options.rationale: Physical facility security is the provider's responsibility in IaaS.

options.text: Maintaining the hypervisor host hardware
options.rationale: The underlying host and hypervisor infrastructure are managed by the provider.

options.text: Powering and cooling the server racks
options.rationale: Environmental controls for the infrastructure are the provider's responsibility.

stem: A stack of DVDs contains highly sensitive archived records that must be disposed of. Since optical media cannot be degaussed, which method is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Physical destruction such as shredding or pulverizing the discs
options.rationale: Optical media is non-magnetic, so physical destruction is the appropriate and highest-assurance disposal method.

options.text: Degaussing the discs
options.rationale: Degaussing has no effect on non-magnetic optical media.

options.text: Deleting the files listed on the discs
options.rationale: Write-once optical media generally cannot be logically wiped, and deletion would not remove burned data anyway.

options.text: Storing them in a locked drawer indefinitely
options.rationale: Retention is not disposal; the sensitive data remains and the requirement to dispose is unmet.

stem: A team deletes a cloud virtual machine but leaves its attached storage volume and snapshots intact and accessible. From a resource-protection standpoint, what is the BEST corrective action?

options.text: Securely delete or crypto-erase the associated volumes and snapshots as part of decommissioning
options.rationale: Decommissioning must include the data artifacts; leaving volumes and snapshots accessible risks exposure of residual sensitive data.

options.text: Leave the volumes and snapshots since the VM is gone
options.rationale: The VM's removal does not sanitize its residual storage; the data remains recoverable.

options.text: Rename the snapshots to obscure them
options.rationale: Renaming does not remove the data or the access risk.

options.text: Increase the VM's memory before deletion
options.rationale: Memory sizing is irrelevant to sanitizing residual cloud storage.

stem: Which factors MOST directly determine the correct media sanitization method to choose?

options.text: The data's sensitivity and whether the media will be reused, released externally, or destroyed
options.rationale: Sanitization selection hinges on classification and the media's fate (internal reuse, external release, or disposal), which map to clear/purge/destroy.

options.text: The color and shape of the media
options.rationale: Physical appearance is irrelevant to the required sanitization level.

options.text: The number of employees in the department
options.rationale: Headcount does not determine sanitization requirements.

options.text: The time of day the disposal occurs
options.rationale: Timing has no bearing on which sanitization method is appropriate.

stem: A company issues laptops that frequently leave the office. Which combination BEST protects the data if a device is lost or stolen?

options.text: Full-disk encryption plus asset tracking so lost devices are known and their data protected
options.rationale: Encryption renders lost-device data unreadable, and asset tracking ensures the organization knows the device is missing and can respond.

options.text: Relying on a login password with an unencrypted disk
options.rationale: A login password can be bypassed by removing the drive; without encryption the data is exposed.

options.text: Placing a company sticker on each laptop
options.rationale: A sticker does not protect data if the device is stolen.

options.text: Disabling the laptop's Wi-Fi permanently
options.rationale: Disabling Wi-Fi does not protect the stored data from a thief with physical possession.
